Photograph: Kevin Dietsch/Getty Images Donald Trump Trump arch could have ‘adverse effects’ on nearby DC monuments, US park service says National Park Service lays out concerns that planned 250ft arch could interfere with historic sites in US capital Ariana Baio Thu 17 Sep 2026 10.46 EDT Last modified on Thu 17 Sep 2026 11.22 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google Donald Trump’s desired triumphal arch in downtown Washington DC will likely contribute “to adverse effects to historic properties”, according to the National Park Service’s planning document , but the construction is still planned to go forward. The president’s 250ft arch could interfere with some of the most well-known views in the nation’s capital, including the symbolic relationship between Arlington House, the Arlington National Cemetery, the Arlington Memorial Bridge and the Lincoln Memorial, which face each other to represent the reunification of the United States after the civil war. As a result, the arch’s construction could require supplemental planning and programming to preserve history, a document and emails obtained by the Washington Post on Wednesday outlined. Kennedy Center to close as Trump threatens to block repairs over name dispute Read more “Such adverse effects cannot be fully avoided while retaining the location-dependent purpose of the undertaking,” the National Park Service wrote in the document. Despite concerns that the arch could interfere with historic sites and would require substantial construction management control, the Trump administration wants to move forward. The document was circulated among preservationists and other groups to review and sign by noon on Monday, according to an email obtained by the Washington Post. The Guardian has asked the National Park Service for comment. Historic preservationists, veterans and lawmakers have consistently raised concerns about the Trump administration building the massive triumphal arch in downtown DC. Veterans filed a lawsuit in September , seeking to halt construction of the arch, believing it would harm the symbolic relationship of historic sites representing the reconciliation of war or disrupt burials at the Arlington National Cemetery. Some lawmakers shared fears that the arch could further complicate DC’s airspace . But Trump has been emphatic about the arch, insisting it should be 250ft high to mark the US’s 250th anniversary. Should construction of the arch move forward, the National Park Service outlined several ways it would mitigate disruptions and potential damage to nearby monuments. That includes installing vibration plates near the Arlington Memorial Bridge and other sensitive sites to ensure construction remains within prescribed limits, enforcing limits on noise-generating activities, prohibiting unnecessary lighting, limiting work hours and more. skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Around 2-3 times a day Sign up to Breaking News US Get the most important news as it breaks after newsletter promotion The National Park Service’s document outlined roughly 37 nearby historic sites that could be affected, including the Lincoln Memorial, the National Mall, the Washington Monument, the Pentagon, the US Capitol and more. But the National Park Service also outlined methods it could implement to preserve the history of the area, such as developing digital programs to explain the commemorative relationship between the Lincoln Memorial and Arlington House, to show before-and-after scenes of the skyline over the Potomac River, and to describe the significance of triumphal arches. Local preservation officers could refuse to sign the agreement, which could trigger another process that involves the Advisory Council on Historic Preservation, a federal agency. However, the Trump administration does not need the preservationists’ consent to move forward because it already received approval from the US Commission on Fine Arts, a federal advisory council made up of Trump appointees, and preliminary approval from the National Capital Planning Commission. https://iranhumanrights.org/2026/10/46-s.text: October 1, 2026 46 States Condemn Iran’s Escalating Use of the Death Penalty at UN Human Rights Council October 1, 2026 — In a significant joint intervention at the UN Human Rights Council, 46 States condemned Iranian authorities’ continued and escalating use of the death penalty , expressing particular concern over the execution of protesters following the state’s brutal crackdown on protests in January. The statement, delivered by Liechtenstein during the Council’s general debate on September 30, 2026, warns that the death penalty is being used to suppress fundamental freedoms and instill fear, while raising serious concerns about due process violations, torture, coerced confessions, and proceedings that fall short of international fair trial standards. No one should face the fear of execution for exercising their rights or seeking to make their voice heard. Iran must immediately halt its abhorrent use of the death penalty. The intervention comes amid mounting international concern over executions linked to the January 2026 protests, with over 30 protesters executed following grossly unfair trials and dozens more at imminent risk of execution. The UN Special Rapporteur on the human rights situation in the Islamic Republic of Iran, Mai Sato, welcomed the joint statement, adding: “The need for a moratorium pending abolition has never been greater.” On July 23, 2026, the UN Independent International Fact-Finding Mission on Iran also called on Iranian authorities to immediately halt all executions, including those in connection with the protests, and establish a moratorium on the use of the death penalty. Read the full statement by over 40 states below. Statement at the 63rd Session of the Human Rights Council General debate under agenda item 8 30 September 2026 Mr. Daniel Batliner Permanent Mission of the Principality of Liechtenstein Thank you, Mister President, I deliver this statement on behalf of over 40 States who strongly condemn the continued and escalating use of the death penalty in Iran. Recent statements by the UN High Commissioner for Human Rights, the Special Rapporteur on Iran, and the findings of the Independent International Fact-Finding Mission on Iran have highlighted a sharp rise in executions and death sentences, particularly in cases linked to protests and the exercise of fundamental freedoms. At least thirty-one protesters have been executed following January’s brutal crackdown by security forces with dozens of protesters sentenced to death and at imminent risk of execution, including women and children. The use of public execution is particularly alarming. We note the findings of UN experts that the death penalty is being used to instill fear, suppress dissent and deter peaceful expression and assembly. We are also concerned by reports that individuals have been sentenced to death following proceedings that appear to fall far short of international fair trial standards, including allegations of closed hearings, denial of due process guarantees, torture and ill-treatment, enforced disappearances, and coerced confessions. No one should face the fear of execution for exercising their rights or seeking to make their voice heard. Iran must immediately halt its abhorrent use of the death penalty. Thank you, Mr. President.
